## Why markets react
International markets respond to **credibility**, **consistency**, and **constraints**. In the simulation, market reactions provide feedback on whether a policy package is plausible.

::: {.callout-note}
Reactions are typically **directional** (up/down/stable) rather than numerical.
:::

## What markets reward
- clear, consistent policy packages
- realistic exchange-rate commitments
- fiscal-monetary coordination
- transparent communication
- credible reforms (especially post-shock)

## What markets punish
- contradictory announcements
- defending an implausible peg
- ignoring balance-of-payments constraints
- repeated policy reversals without justification

## Common outcomes we will report
- exchange-rate movement (appreciation/depreciation)
- capital flows (inflows/outflows)
- borrowing conditions (spreads tighten/widen)
- trade effects (improving/deteriorating)
- spillovers to other countries


## FAQs

### How much math is required?
Very little. You will use basic arithmetic for exchange-rate changes, trade balances, and simple comparisons. The focus is on reasoning.

### Can my country fail?
Absolutely. Your country can experience severe stress (currency collapse, loss of market access, etc.). That is part of the learning. But you are not graded on outcomes.

### What if markets react badly?
You respond with a new policy package. Markets reward coherence and credible reforms.

### Do we need to predict exact exchange rates?
No. Outcomes are reported directionally (appreciation/depreciation; inflows/outflows).


### How do submissions work?
All submissions go through Canvas. See: [Deliverables](deliverables.qmd)
